desc:
Browser extension MVP development from Ecom Swift LLC turns a rough idea into a focused first version you can put in front of real testers, so you learn what people want before you invest in the full product.

## What is a browser extension MVP?

A browser extension MVP, short for minimum viable product, is the smallest working version of your extension that still does one useful job. It is not a demo or a mock-up. It installs, runs on real pages and can be used by real people, but it leaves out everything that is not needed to test the idea.

The point is learning. You want to know whether anyone will install the tool, use it twice and tell a friend. Building the full version first answers that question slowly and at high cost.

## Why a small first version protects your budget

Founders often discover that the feature they loved is not the one users want. A small build lets that discovery happen early, while changing direction is cheap. It also gets you a working link to share, which is far more persuasive to testers, partners and early customers than a description.

A narrow scope also means fewer permissions, a simpler store review and less to maintain. When a feature is proven, it can grow. When it is not, you have spent a small amount to find out.

## What a good extension MVP includes

- One core job, described in a single sentence and agreed in writing.
- A single popup or a small set of screens, with nothing decorative.
- Settings and data saved in the browser, so no account is required at first.
- A build that testers can load without the store, or a private release.
- Privacy-friendly usage counts that show which actions people take.
- A feedback link or form, so testers can tell you what they think.
- Clear default behavior, so a new user succeeds without instructions.
- A permission list kept as short as the job allows.
- Source code you own, organized so a developer can extend it.
- A short list of what was left out on purpose, and why.

## How we shape and build it

We begin with a short conversation about your idea, your audience and the problem you want to solve. Together we cut the idea down to the job that matters most, and we write it as a feature list you approve. Then we build, test on real pages and prepare the build for your testers.

The packages scale from a first test to a launch-ready version. Basic delivers one job in one popup with a loadable test build. Standard handles up to two jobs, an options page, usage counts, a feedback link and a store-ready package. Premium adds sign-in, cloud storage, basic free and paid limits, store listing text and a roadmap for what to build next.

## Do and avoid when testing an idea

**Do:**
- Pick one audience and talk to a few of them first.
- Decide what result would make you continue.
- Ask testers to complete one task and watch how they do it.
- Read feedback in batches, not one message at a time.
- Keep the next step small and clear.

**Avoid:**
- Adding settings nobody asked for.
- Judging the idea from three friendly opinions.
- Building accounts before you know the tool is wanted.
- Collecting more data than the question requires.
- Treating a quiet week as proof of failure without checking how many people actually saw it.

## Who this is for

It suits a first-time founder with an idea for a tool that lives next to the web pages people already use. It suits a business that wants to test a customer-facing helper before committing a larger budget. And it suits a creator with an audience who wants to give them a small free tool and see what happens.

## What we need from you

Send a short description of the idea, the people it is for and the websites or tasks involved. If you have sketches, examples of similar tools or brand colors, share them. Tell us how you plan to find testers.

We never ask for passwords. You can add us to your code repository or receive the files by zip. For a store release, create your own developer account and we explain each step. After you order, we reply with a scoping note to approve first.
